5. 
Agertcies, Courts, and Scientific Policymaking. The Benzene Case 
illustrates the uncertainties in assessing risk. In deciding whether to reduce 
worker exposure to benzene, OSHA was confronted with a difficulty. Scientists 
had evidence from epidemiological studies—observational studies of exposed 
populations—that benzene at high levels increased the “natural” or 
“background” incidence of leukemia. To be sure, some workers in almost any 
work environment would “naturally” experience leukemia even if they were 
not exposed to benzene. But, as is often the case, the exposures demonstrated 
to cause leukemia eventually in a few workers were considerably higher than 
those currently being experienced. It would take a long time to find out, from 
observing workers currently exposed, whether the levels allowed by any given 
standard would cause any additional cases of leukemia, much less how many.
If OSHA had possessed good information about the levels of exposure that 
had been shown to cause cancer, it might have been able to construct what is 
called a “dose-response curve” from which it could project the possible 
increased incidence of cancer at lower levels. But this information was missing; 
OSHA did not have the option of relying on experimental results in animals 
because the few experiments on benzene had not shown it to be carcinogenic 
at any level. OSHA had concluded that, for any compound shown capable of 
causing cancer, no safe, or “threshold” dose could be presumed. That is, any 
exposure to the compound creates some risk of causing cancer.
Quantitative risk assessment for carcinogens inevitably incorporates a 
host of assumptions that cannot be proved and rehes on data that are almost 
always incomplete. For instance, one might not know that: the “no threshold” 
assumption holds for many chemicals; laboratory animals are always good 
surrogates for humans, or, if two species have been tested, which species 
should be assumed to be the closer match; or the dose-response relationship is 
the same for animals and humans, or the same for humans throughout the 
range of possible exposures. We often lack good information about how much 
of a chemical humans are actually exposed to, so that any estimate of the risk 
they face is in a real sense speculative. And we lack good information about 
the interactions among different chemicals that may create compounding 
effects from exposure to both. In short, extrapolations from responses to high 
levels of exposure to low levels or exposure, or from studies of animal exposure, 
incorporate many assumptions about the shape of a dose-response curve as 
well as uncertainty within the available data. Uncertainty is thus a pervasive 
characteristic of regulatory risk assessments. But the technique continues to 
be used because there are no better alternatives.
